responses.answer: I’d start by slowing the conversation down and clarifying exactly what the customer is seeing. I’d ask them to walk me through what happened from the point they expected the booking to be there, and whether the issue is that they can’t see the appointment at all, the booking looks changed, or they can’t access it in the way they expected. Because their account shows several recent changes, I’d also check what service or outcome is actually affected — for example, whether the appointment was removed, rescheduled, or just not reflected in the latest notification. Then I’d summarise it back to them in plain terms, such as: ‘So the main issue is that your online appointment is missing even though you received a confirmation, and we need to confirm which booking is currently active before we go further.’ That way I know I’m solving the right problem before choosing next steps.

I’d first get them to talk me through what they’re seeing, because I want to pin down the exact problem rather than guess. I’d ask whether the booking is missing completely, whether it shows up under a different time, or whether the confirmation they got doesn’t match what’s in the account. Since there have been recent changes, I’d check what part of the service is actually affected and how that’s impacting the appointment itself. Then I’d repeat it back to make sure I’ve got it right — something like, ‘It sounds like the confirmed booking isn’t showing as expected, and we need to confirm whether it was changed or replaced before I help further.’

I’d ask them to describe exactly what they can and can’t see, check whether the appointment itself is missing or just changed, and confirm what impact that has on the upcoming visit. Then I’d restate the problem back to them — for example, that the confirmed booking isn’t appearing as expected and we need to verify which booking is active.

I’d begin by asking the customer what they expected to see and what they are seeing now, so I can narrow down whether the booking is missing, altered, or duplicated. I’d also look at the recent changes on the account to understand whether the online appointment is affected or whether only the confirmation message is out of date. Once I have that, I’d confirm the general issue with them before moving to a fix, so I’m not making assumptions about what went wrong.

I’d ask them to explain what happened and what they see on their side, because I’d want to figure out whether the booking disappeared, moved, or just isn’t showing properly. I’d also check the recent account changes to understand what part of the process has been affected. After that I’d make sure I’ve got the issue broadly right before I pick a next step.

I’d ask what they expected to see, what’s showing now, and review the recent booking changes to understand whether the appointment itself or just the confirmation is affected. Then I’d confirm the issue before choosing a fix.

I’d probably treat it as a standard booking error and start by re-sending the confirmation or looking for a duplicate appointment in the system. If the customer says it’s missing, that usually means the original booking didn’t go through properly, so I’d focus on restoring the booking details first. I wouldn’t spend too long digging into the customer’s explanation unless the system shows something unusual, because the quickest path is usually to correct the booking record and then let them know the appointment is back in place.

I’d assume it’s mainly a confirmation problem and get straight into checking whether the email or notification needs to be sent again. If there’s no booking showing, I’d just look for the most recent record and try to restore that, since the customer’s probably just seeing an old message. I’d only ask more questions if the account looked really unusual.

I’d start by checking the latest booking record and reissuing the confirmation if needed, since this sounds like a confirmation mismatch. If the appointment is missing, I’d focus on restoring it rather than spending much time clarifying the details first.
